mcq.q: A support team wants to check that every purchase order has a valid PO number. What fits best?
options: An LLM with few-shot examples
A deterministic rule
A fine-tuned classifier
An agent with tools
mcq.why: The logic is explicit and must be exact, so a rule is cheaper, auditable and correct every time.
distractors: An LLM follows examples but is not exact; a PO-number check must be right every time and cost almost nothing.
A classifier needs labels and returns a probability; the PO-number format is explicit logic, not a prediction.
An agent adds a loop, tools and cost around what is a single deterministic check.

mcq.q: In an insurance claims intake, which question is best answered by search?
options: Is this claim likely fraudulent?
Turn the customer's email into the claim form
Is the policy active on the incident date?
Which clause covers water damage?
mcq.why: The answer already exists in a document; users need to find it, with the source shown.
distractors: That is a prediction from claim history: traditional ML.
That is extraction from free text: an LLM with validation.
That is a database lookup and a date comparison: a rule.

mcq.q: “Is the policy active on the incident date?” is best handled by…
options: A web search for the policy's public terms
An LLM reading the policy and the incident
A rule: a database query and a date comparison
A clustering model trained on past policies
mcq.why: The logic can be written down and must be exact, so code is deterministic, auditable and free to run.
distractors: The answer is in your own records, not on the web.
An exact date check needs no language model, and an LLM could get it wrong.
Clustering groups similar items; it cannot say whether a date falls in a range.

mcq.q: “Is this claim likely fraudulent?”, with years of labelled claim history, is a job for…
options: Keyword search over past claim notes
An LLM prompt with the fraud policy
A hand-written rule for each fraud type
Traditional ML on structured claim data
mcq.why: Tabular data, a fixed output and plenty of labels fit traditional ML, which gives cheap, calibrated scores.
distractors: Search finds documents; it does not estimate a likelihood.
With years of labels, a trained model is cheaper, measurable and calibrated; an LLM is none of these here.
Fraud patterns change and overlap; written rules are brittle and miss what they did not anticipate.

mcq.q: “Turn the customer's long email into the structured claim form” is a job for…
options: A rule that copies the email text into the form's free-text field
Search over past claims for the most similar form already filled in
Traditional ML that predicts each form field from the email's length
An LLM, with schema validation and rules that check the extracted amounts
mcq.why: Free text in, structured fields out is what LLMs do well, but the output must be validated (7.4) and checked by rules.
distractors: Copying text does not fill the structured fields the form needs.
A similar old claim has different facts; the form must come from this email.
Email length carries no information about the fields' values.

mcq.q: According to the topic, what is the most expensive mistake in enterprise AI?
options: Using an LLM where a simpler tool is more accurate, cheaper and easier to audit
Using rules for permissions, where a model would adapt to new roles better
Measuring a baseline before building, which delays the first release
Showing sources in search results, which makes users read instead of ask
mcq.why: LLMs add cost, latency and risk; when a simpler method fits, it usually wins on all three.
distractors: Permissions must be exact and auditable, which is what rules are for.
A baseline is how you know whether a model helps at all.
Showing sources is one of search's strengths.

mcq.q: Which are strengths of search as an approach?
options: It learns from labels, so it improves with each query
It handles vague queries better than any other tool
It writes new text that combines several documents
It shows sources, is fast and does not fabricate
mcq.why: Search returns existing documents, so answers are traceable. Its weakness is that users must read and synthesise, and vague queries do poorly.
distractors: Learning from labels describes traditional ML, not search.
Vague queries are one of search's weaknesses.
Writing new text is an LLM's job; search returns existing documents.

mcq.q: When does traditional ML fit best?
options: Exact tax calculations that must give the same result every time
Structured or tabular data, a fixed set of outputs and plenty of labels
Open-ended drafting of letters and replies from a short brief
Finding a policy document that a user describes in their own words
mcq.why: Churn, fraud and demand forecasts are typical: cheap at scale, measurable and calibrated.
distractors: Exact logic that can be written down belongs in rules.
Open-ended text is an LLM job; traditional ML does not generate text.
Finding a document is a search task.

mcq.q: Which of these are weaknesses of using an LLM? Choose all that apply.
options: Risk of prompt injection
It cannot handle varied wording
Non-determinism
Cost and latency
mcq.why: LLMs handle variety well; their costs are price, speed, randomness, hallucination and injection risk.
distractors: Handling varied wording is one of their strengths.

mcq.q: A team chooses an agent framework first and then looks for a problem to use it on. What is wrong with this?
options: It reverses the decision: start from the task and the simplest tool that fits
Agents cannot call tools reliably, so the framework adds no new capability
Nothing: a framework is always needed before any problem is chosen
Frameworks are too cheap to signal a serious investment to leadership
mcq.why: Problem selection asks what the task really is; the tool follows.
distractors: Agents do call tools; the problem is choosing the tool before the task.
Many tasks need no framework at all; a rule or search may fit better.
Cost signalling is not a reason to pick a tool; fit to the task is.

interview.q: How do you decide between rules, search, traditional ML and an LLM for a new problem?
covers: What the task really is: exact logic, finding, predicting or generating
Data and labels available
Cost of a wrong answer and auditability
Latency and volume
Start with the simplest tool that fits
interview.followUp: Walk me through that decision for one task you have worked on.

interview.q: Why do most real systems combine several of these approaches?
covers: Each does a different job well
Search finds facts, an LLM phrases, rules enforce limits
Combination adds components to monitor
Boundaries make failures traceable
interview.followUp: What does combining them cost, and how do you keep that manageable?

interview.q: Split an insurance claims intake into components and justify each choice.
covers: Policy active on the date: rule
Which clause applies: search
Fraud likelihood: trained model
Email to form: LLM with validation and checks
interview.followUp: The fraud score and the LLM-extracted amount point different ways. Which decides, and why?

interview.q: Split {company}'s change-request flow into rule, search, model and LLM parts, and explain each choice.
covers: Fare-rule arithmetic and deadlines: rules
Finding the fare and hotel terms: search
Cancellation-risk pricing: a trained model
Understanding the traveller's message: an LLM
interview.followUp: Which of those parts would you build first, and why?

interview.q: When would you not use an LLM even though it could do the task?
covers: When exact, auditable answers are required
When labels exist and a small model is cheaper
At very high volume with tight latency
When the data must not leave a boundary
interview.followUp: The team says the LLM is good enough. What evidence would settle it?

interview.q: Design an expense-approval assistant.
covers: Rules for limits and eligibility
Search over the expense policy
A trained model for fraud risk
An LLM to explain decisions
Approvals, logging and an evaluation set
interview.followUp: Which part would you build and test first?

interview.q: Design dispute handling for {company} so that every decision can be reproduced months later.
covers: Deterministic rules for deadlines and eligibility, versioned
Model scores logged with model version and threshold
LLM used for summaries and letters, not decisions
Inputs, outputs and versions captured per case
Human approval for refunds above a limit
interview.followUp: A customer disputes a decision from eight months ago. Walk me through reproducing it.

interview.q: A stakeholder insists on “an agent” for a problem that is a lookup. How do you handle it?
covers: Restate the task and its requirements
Show the simpler solution's accuracy, cost and latency
Explain the agent's added risks
Offer an LLM where it adds value, such as phrasing
interview.followUp: The stakeholder says an agent will be needed later anyway. How do you respond?

mcq.q: Why can an LLM state a wrong invoice due date fluently?
options: It looked the date up in a stale database that it was connected to
It predicts a likely continuation, which need not be true
Its temperature was too low, so it repeated the most common due date
Its context window was too small to hold the rest of the conversation
mcq.why: Generation picks plausible tokens; without the invoice in context, a plausible date is still the likely continuation.
distractors: A bare LLM looks nothing up; without the invoice in context it can only produce a likely-looking date.
Low temperature makes output more consistent, not wrong; the cause is predicting what is likely rather than true.
A small window can drop facts, but the root cause is that a plausible date is still the likely continuation.

mcq.q: At each step, what does a modern language model output?
options: The single correct next word, chosen by a rule
A ranked list of web pages that match the text
A database row that matches the question asked
A probability for every token in its vocabulary
mcq.why: Given the text so far, the model outputs a probability distribution over its whole vocabulary; generation picks one token and repeats.
distractors: The model outputs a distribution; a decoding rule then picks a token, and it need not be correct.
Search engines return pages; a language model returns token probabilities.
Nothing in the model is a database row; knowledge is spread across weights.

mcq.q: Answering a question, writing code and summarising a document are, for an LLM, all…
options: Separate skills that engineers hard-code into the model after training
Separate algorithms in separate modules, chosen by a router per request
Continuing text in a way that is likely given everything before it
Lookups in a knowledge base that was built during pretraining
mcq.why: The core mechanism is the same continuation; instruction tuning makes a helpful answer the likely continuation of a question.
distractors: No task is hard-coded; every task is next-token prediction.
One model runs one operation for all of them: predict the next token.
Pretraining spreads associations across weights; there is no knowledge base to look up.

mcq.q: Which three things together usually make a model an LLM?
options: Any neural network that reads text, with a tokenizer and a vocabulary
A transformer, many parameters and pretraining on a broad, very large corpus
A chatbot interface, a system prompt and a conversation history store
Exactly one billion parameters, a GPU cluster and a context window
mcq.why: The term combines architecture, scale and broad pretraining; there is no agreed parameter cut-off.
distractors: A small text classifier has a tokenizer too; scale and broad pretraining are what make it large.
Those are parts of an application, not of the model.
There is no agreed parameter cut-off, and hardware does not define the model.

mcq.q: Which statement about parameter count is correct?
options: Above 10 billion parameters a model no longer hallucinates on facts
Parameter count is the same number as the model's context length
More parameters always give better answers on every task and dataset
It alone does not measure quality; data, training and the task matter as much
mcq.why: Parameter count is one factor. Data, training objectives and adaptation strongly affect quality.
distractors: No size removes hallucination; it comes from predicting what is likely.
Parameters are learned weights; context length is how many tokens fit in the input and output.
A smaller, better-trained or task-adapted model often beats a larger one.

mcq.q: In the illustrative example, why does “March” get the highest probability after “The invoice is due on the 15th of”?
options: March is the current month, which the model reads from the system clock
The tokenizer prefers short words, so shorter month names score higher
The model looked the invoice up and found that it is due in March
It is a common continuation, not because the model knows the invoice
mcq.why: The model ranks likely text; it has no access to your invoice unless it is in the context. The gap between likely and true is the root of hallucination.
distractors: The model has no clock; it only sees the text in its context.
The tokenizer splits text; it does not score continuations.
Nothing was looked up; no invoice was in the context.

mcq.q: Where is the knowledge that “Canberra” follows “capital of Australia” stored?
options: In the tokenizer's vocabulary, as a token that joins the two words
Spread across billions of weights as learned associations
In the system prompt that the provider adds to every request
In a table row labelled “capital of Australia” inside the model
mcq.why: There is no database row; the association is distributed across the model's parameters.
distractors: The vocabulary is a list of text pieces with IDs; it stores no facts.
The model answers this without any prompt saying so; the association is in the weights.
There is no table inside the model; that is the misconception the topic warns against.

mcq.q: Why do some abilities appear only in larger models?
options: Some tasks, like new formats or rare translations, only become reliable above a certain scale
Large models use different mathematics, such as symbolic logic, in their upper layers
Small models cannot read text directly, so they need a larger model to tokenise it
Abilities depend only on the prompt; a larger model just reads longer prompts
mcq.why: Scale (with data) makes some abilities reliable; the “large” in LLM matters for that reason.
distractors: Small and large transformers run the same operations; only the scale differs.
Every model has its own tokenizer; size does not change how text is read.
The same prompt works on one size and fails on another, so scale matters, not just the prompt.

mcq.q: What does instruction tuning change?
options: It removes next-token prediction and replaces it with answer lookup
It turns the model into a database of approved question-answer pairs
It makes a helpful answer the likely continuation of a user's question
It guarantees factual answers by training on verified instructions
mcq.why: Instruction-tuned models still predict continuations; tuning shapes which continuations are likely.
distractors: Instruction-tuned models still predict continuations.
Instruction tuning adjusts weights; it does not store answers to look up.
Tuned models still hallucinate; the likely answer need not be true.

mcq.q: Which design choice best addresses the “likely is not true” gap for questions about your own records?
options: Lower the temperature to zero so the answer is always the same
Retrieve the record and require the answer to cite it
Use a larger model that has memorised more of your records
Add “be careful and only state facts” to the system prompt
mcq.why: Only supplying the facts and requiring citations closes the gap; bigger models and lower temperature still guess when facts are missing.
distractors: Consistent is not correct: the same likely-but-wrong answer every time.
Your records were never in its training data, and memorised facts are unattributable.
An instruction cannot supply a fact the model does not have.

mcq.q: In an illustrative next-token distribution after “The invoice is due on the 15th of”, “␣March” has 0.30, “␣each” 0.20 and “␣every” 0.15. Which statement is correct?
options: There is a 30% chance that this particular invoice is really due in March
The probabilities need not sum to 1, so the remaining share is unknown
All other tokens hold 0, because the model keeps only its top three tokens
All other tokens together hold 0.35, and March leads without knowing the invoice
mcq.why: The model gives every vocabulary token a probability, and they sum to 1: 1 − (0.30 + 0.20 + 0.15) = 0.35 for everything else. A high probability means a common continuation, not a fact about this invoice.
distractors: 0.30 is how likely the text continues with “March”, not how likely the invoice is due then; no invoice is in the context.
Softmax makes the probabilities sum to 1, so the rest is exactly 0.35.
The model outputs a probability for every token in its vocabulary; a decoding rule may sample from fewer, but the distribution covers all.

mcq.q: A team sends “What is our refund window?” to a base model that has not been instruction-tuned. It replies with three more questions in the same style. What explains this?
options: For an untuned model, more questions were a likelier continuation than an answer
The context window was full, so the model never saw the question itself
Its temperature was zero, which makes any model repeat the input's format
The model refused, because the question was about the company's own policy
mcq.why: Every task is continuation. Instruction tuning is what makes a helpful answer the likely continuation of a question; a base model may continue the text as a list of questions.
distractors: A one-line prompt does not fill a context window, and the questions it wrote follow the prompt's style.
Temperature changes how a token is picked from the distribution, not which kind of continuation is likely.
Writing more questions is not a refusal; the model continued the text in its likeliest form.

interview.q: Explain what a language model actually predicts, in one minute.
covers: A probability distribution over the next token given the text so far
Generation repeats: pick a token, append, predict again
All tasks are continuation
Instruction tuning shapes which continuations are likely
interview.followUp: If every task is continuation, why can the same prompt give different answers on two runs?

interview.q: What makes a model “large”, and is parameter count a good measure of quality?
covers: Transformer architecture, many parameters and broad pretraining together
No fixed threshold
Data, objectives and adaptation matter as much as size
Scale makes some abilities reliable
interview.followUp: How would you compare two models of different sizes on your own task?

interview.q: Why do LLMs hallucinate, from first principles?
covers: They output what is likely, not what is verified
Missing facts still yield a likely-looking answer
Facts are spread across weights, not looked up
Mitigation needs grounding and verification
interview.followUp: Does retrieval remove hallucination completely? Why not?

interview.q: A user says the assistant “knew” their order status yesterday but not today. What is likely happening?
covers: The model has no memory of their records
Yesterday the context probably contained the order
Retrieval or tool calls may have failed today
Check logs of what was in the context
interview.followUp: Which logs would you check first, and what would you expect them to show?

interview.q: How would you test whether a model is guessing instead of answering from provided facts?
covers: Ask about facts deliberately absent from the context
Ask about records that do not exist
Check citations against the source
Measure refusal or “not stated” rates
interview.followUp: How would you make the model say “I don't know” more often without making it unhelpful?

interview.q: {company}'s assistant quoted a wrong fixed-deposit penalty. Explain to a compliance officer why this happened and what you will change.
covers: Model produced a likely number without the policy in context
Retrieval missed or returned an outdated policy
Require quoting the current policy and citing it
Block numeric answers without a source
Add the case to the evaluation set
interview.followUp: The compliance officer asks how you will know it is fixed. What do you measure?

interview.q: Design an answer flow that never states an account or invoice detail it cannot cite.
covers: Retrieve records with the user's permissions
Pass them with IDs into the context
Require citations for each claim
Verify claims against retrieved text before sending
Fallback wording when nothing is found
interview.followUp: How would you check that a cited passage really supports the claim, at production volume?

interview.q: How would you explain to a product team that an LLM is not a knowledge base, and what architecture follows from that?
covers: Knowledge in weights is approximate, undated and unattributable
Facts that must be right live in systems of record
Retrieval and tools supply them at question time
The model phrases and reasons over supplied facts
interview.followUp: Which questions would you still let the model answer from its own weights?

mcq.q: What changes the model's weights?
options: A long conversation
A better system prompt
Training or fine-tuning
Retrieval
mcq.why: Only training updates parameters. Prompts, chats and retrieved text change the input only.
distractors: A conversation only changes the input; the weights stay fixed however long it runs.
A system prompt is part of the input; it steers behaviour without changing any parameter.
Retrieval adds documents to the context; the model reads them but does not learn from them.

mcq.q: Using the English-prose rule of thumb (1 token ≈ 0.75 words), about how many tokens is a 3,000-word document?
mcq.why: Tokens ≈ words ÷ 0.75, so 3,000 ÷ 0.75 = 4,000. Confirm with the model's own tokenizer, because other languages, code and numbers differ.
distractors: That assumes one token per word; common words are one token, but many words split.
That multiplies by 0.75 instead of dividing: there are more tokens than words.
That treats each word as four tokens; four is roughly characters per token, not tokens per word.

mcq.q: A call sends 4,000 input tokens at $1 per million and receives 270 output tokens at $4 per million (illustrative prices). What does it cost?
options: About $4.27
About $0.005
About $0.004
About $0.05
distractors: That forgets to divide by one million.
That counts only the input tokens.
That is ten times too high; check the powers of ten.

mcq.q: At about $0.005 per summary, what do 100,000 summaries a month cost?
options: About $500
About $0.50
About $5,000
About $50
mcq.why: 100,000 × $0.005 = $500 a month (illustrative prices).
distractors: That divides instead of multiplying.
That is a factor of ten too high.
That is a factor of ten too low.

mcq.q: What is an embedding?
options: A compressed copy of the text that can be decoded back to the exact original
The file that stores the model's weights, including its embedding table
A vector of numbers that represents text, with similar meanings close together
The integer ID that the tokenizer gives each token in its vocabulary
mcq.why: An embedding places text in a vector space where related meanings are near each other. It is not a reversible compression of the text.
distractors: You cannot reliably decode the original document from an embedding.
The embedding table is part of the weights; an embedding is one vector from it, or for a piece of text.
The token ID selects a row; the vector in that row is the embedding.

mcq.q: What does the context window limit?
options: The number of requests per minute that the provider accepts from one key
The size of the vocabulary, the number of distinct tokens it can produce
The number of parameters that are active for each token it processes
The total number of input and output tokens the model can consider at once
mcq.why: Everything outside the context window is invisible to the model, and the output must fit in it too.
distractors: That is a rate limit, set by the provider, not by the model.
Vocabulary size is fixed by the tokenizer and unrelated to how much text fits at once.
Parameters are the learned weights; the window is about tokens.

mcq.q: Why should you count tokens with the model's own tokenizer rather than converting from words?
options: Prices are charged per word, so a word count is what the invoice uses
Words and tokens are identical in English, the language prices use
Every model uses the same tokenizer, so a fixed ratio is always exact
Token counts vary widely with language, code, numbers and tokenizer
mcq.why: The four-characters-per-token rule is a rough English average; other text and other tokenizers can differ a lot.
distractors: Prices, speed and limits are all counted in tokens.
Even in English a token is about 0.75 words on average, and only on average.
Tokenizers differ between models; the same text gives different counts.

mcq.q: A chat product “remembers” a user's preference across sessions. Where does that memory live?
options: In the model's weights, which update a little after every chat
In the GPU's memory, where the session's state stays loaded
In the tokenizer's vocabulary, which adds the user's new terms
In application storage that is put back into the context
mcq.why: Prompting never changes the weights. “Memory” is stored by the application and re-sent as text (7.5).
distractors: Chatting never changes weights; only training does.
Serving memory is shared and freed between requests; nothing personal persists there.
The vocabulary is fixed when the tokenizer is built.

mcq.q: Why does output length usually dominate latency?
options: Output tokens are computed in advance and cached, so input reading waits for them
Input tokens are skipped after the first layer, so only output tokens use compute
Output tokens are generated one at a time, while input tokens are read in parallel
Output tokens are cheaper to compute, so providers queue them behind input tokens
mcq.why: The prompt is processed in one parallel pass; each output token needs another step through the model.
distractors: Output cannot be computed before the input is read; each output token depends on the ones before it.
Every input token passes through every layer; it is just done in one parallel pass.
Output tokens are usually priced higher, and the delay comes from generating them one by one.

mcq.q: A request uses a 900-token system prompt, 2,500 tokens of passages, 600 tokens of history and an 800-token output reserve, within a 5,000-token budget. If history grows to 1,000 tokens, what happens?
options: It no longer fits: it is 1,000 tokens over
It no longer fits: it is 200 tokens over
It fits, because the output reserve does not count
It still fits with room to spare
mcq.why: 900 + 2,500 + 1,000 + 800 = 5,200 tokens, 200 over the 5,000 budget, so something must be trimmed or summarised.
distractors: Only the 400-token growth was added, giving 200 over, not 1,000.
The output must fit in the same window as the input.
The total is 5,200, which exceeds 5,000.

interview.q: Explain tokens, parameters, embeddings and the context window, and how they relate in one request.
covers: Tokens are units of text with integer IDs
Embeddings are vectors looked up for each token
Parameters are the learned numbers that transform them
The context window caps input plus output tokens
interview.followUp: Which of these drive cost, and which drive latency?

interview.q: Walk through what happens in one inference step, from text to the next token.
covers: Tokenise, map to IDs
Look up embeddings
Pass through transformer layers
Logits, softmax, decode one token, append and repeat
interview.followUp: Which of these steps differ during training, and which stay the same?

interview.q: What is the difference between training and inference, and which do most engineers work with?
covers: Training changes weights from data and is expensive
Inference uses fixed weights and is cheap per call
Prompting never changes weights
Most product work is inference
interview.followUp: When would a product team need to fine-tune rather than prompt?

interview.q: Estimate the monthly cost of a feature that summarises 100,000 three-thousand-word documents into 200-word summaries.
covers: Convert words to tokens and confirm with a tokenizer
Separate input and output prices
Compute cost per call, then per month
Note that output length drives latency
State the assumptions and how sensitive the result is
interview.followUp: Which assumption would you check first, and how?

interview.q: A user says the assistant forgot something they said fifty messages ago. Explain why and what you would change.
covers: The context window has a limit
Old turns were truncated or summarised away
Memory is application storage, not weights
Options: summaries, retrieval over history, pinned facts
interview.followUp: How would you choose between summarising old turns and retrieving from them?

interview.q: {assistant} handles English, Hindi, Tamil and Hinglish requests. How would you budget tokens and cost per language?
covers: Measure token counts per language with the real tokenizer
Look at the distribution, not one example
Separate input from output length
Price per language and per request type
Monitor as the language mix changes
interview.followUp: Hinglish requests use far more tokens than you budgeted. What do you change first?

interview.q: Design a context budget for an assistant with a system prompt, retrieved passages, conversation history and an answer.
covers: Fixed reserves for system prompt and output
Priority order for what is trimmed first
Summarising or retrieving history instead of sending all of it
Counting with the tokenizer at runtime
Logging token use per component
interview.followUp: On long chats the retrieved passages crowd out the history. What do you trim, and how do you check it was the right choice?

interview.q: Festival-sale traffic will be forty times normal. How do token budgets change your cost and latency plan for {assistant}?
covers: Cost scales with tokens per request times volume
Trim retrieved text and cap output length
Cache shared prompt prefixes
Route simple requests to a cheaper model
Load-test with realistic prompts
interview.followUp: Which of those levers would you try first, and how would you check that answer quality held?

mcq.q: Which statement about AI, ML, deep learning and generative AI is correct?
options: Every LLM is generative, deep and machine-learned
Machine learning excludes neural networks
Every generative model ever built is a deep learning model
Hand-written rules do not count as AI
mcq.why: The four terms are nested sets. An LLM sits inside all of them, so it inherits the outer sets' concerns: it needs data, can overfit and behaves statistically.
distractors: Neural networks are one family of ML methods; deep learning sits inside ML.
Almost all of today's generative AI is deep learning, but the definition does not require it; older generative models such as n-gram language models are not deep.
Rules count as AI when they perform a task we would call intelligent if a person did it.

mcq.q: In classical machine learning, where do the input features usually come from?
options: They are copied from a pretraining corpus
The engineer chooses and computes them
The model's hidden layers learn them
They are written as IF–THEN rules
mcq.why: Classical ML learns weights from labelled examples, but an engineer decides the features, such as word counts or “amount above average”.
distractors: Pretraining corpora belong to foundation models, not classical feature design.
Learning features in hidden layers is what distinguishes deep learning.
IF–THEN rules are rule-based AI, where nothing is learned.

mcq.q: You must route 20,000 already-labelled support emails into eight fixed teams, cheaply and quickly. Which approach does the topic's example describe as cheap, fast and accurate on common categories?
options: Prompting a large LLM for every email
Only hand-written keyword rules
TF-IDF word features with logistic regression
Training a transformer from scratch
mcq.why: With plenty of labels and a fixed label set, a classical classifier is cheap to run and accurate on common categories.
distractors: An LLM works with zero training data, but costs more per email and its label must be validated; with 20,000 labels you can do better cheaply.
Rules are transparent but brittle when wording changes.
Training a transformer from scratch needs far more data and compute than this task justifies.

mcq.q: Why is generative output harder to evaluate than a classifier's output?
options: Generative models are always less accurate
Generative models do not produce probabilities
There is usually no single correct answer to compare against
Generative output cannot be measured at all
mcq.why: A label can be compared with the right label. A drafted reply can be correct in many wordings, so it needs rubrics, checks or human and model judges (chapter 8).
distractors: Generative models can be very accurate; the difficulty is in verifying open-ended output.
LLMs output a probability for every token; that does not make open-ended text easy to grade.
It can be measured, with more effort: rubrics, groundedness checks and human review.

mcq.q: You use an LLM to label emails with a team name. What check does the topic say you must add?
options: Ask the model to report how confident it is in each label it returns
Validate that the returned label is one of the allowed values
Raise the temperature so the model explores more possible team labels
Retrain the LLM every week on the emails it labelled the week before
mcq.why: Open-ended output can contain anything, so an application must check that the label is from the allowed set before acting on it.
distractors: Self-reported confidence does not track correctness (1.5), and it cannot catch an invented team name.
Higher temperature adds randomness, which makes an off-list label more likely, not less.
Training on its own unchecked labels reinforces its mistakes and still does not guarantee a valid label.

mcq.q: Which of these is deep learning but not generative AI?
options: A chat LLM that drafts replies to the same incoming emails
A hand-written keyword rule that routes invoice emails to Billing
Logistic regression trained on TF-IDF word features of the emails
A fine-tuned BERT-style encoder that classifies emails
mcq.why: An encoder classifier is a deep network, but it outputs a label from a fixed set rather than new content.
distractors: A chat LLM is deep learning and generative: it produces open-ended text.
A keyword rule is AI, but nothing is learned, so it is not ML at all.
Logistic regression on chosen features is classical ML: no deep network learns the features.

mcq.q: Which concerns does an LLM inherit from the outer sets (machine learning and deep learning)? Choose all that apply.
options: Its output is guaranteed to be deterministic
Its behaviour is statistical
It needs training data
It can overfit
mcq.why: As a machine-learned, deep model, an LLM needs data, can overfit and behaves statistically.
distractors: Sampling makes output vary, and even greedy decoding can differ across hardware; nothing guarantees determinism.

mcq.q: A team calls its whole pipeline “the AI”, and a wrong answer reaches a customer. What does naming each component (rules, search, reranker, LLM) make possible?
options: Skipping evaluation, since each named component is already tested alone
Making the LLM deterministic, because each component has a fixed role
Tracing which component caused the error and what it cost
Dropping request logs, because component names already explain failures
mcq.why: Separate components have separate failure modes and costs. Naming them lets you log, measure and fix each one.
distractors: Named parts still need evaluation, alone and together; naming makes the results attributable, not unnecessary.
Naming components changes nothing about how the LLM samples tokens.
Names are only useful with per-component logs; without logs a bad answer cannot be traced.

mcq.q: In a rule-based AI system, where does the knowledge come from?
options: The programmer who writes the rules
Labelled examples the system was fitted to
Feedback that users give on its answers
Patterns learned from a pretraining corpus
mcq.why: Rule-based systems encode a person's knowledge directly as rules; nothing is learned from data.
distractors: Learning from labelled examples is machine learning, not rules.
A rule-based system does not change from feedback unless a person rewrites the rules.
Pretraining on a corpus is how large neural models learn, not rule-based systems.

mcq.q: For a fixed labelling task with plenty of labelled data, which statement matches the topic's warning?
options: A small classifier can beat a generative model on cost and accuracy
Rules can never be part of the solution once labelled data exists
Deep learning is required because labelled data is already plentiful
A generative model is the best choice because it needs no training
mcq.why: A generative model is not automatically better than a small classifier when the output is a fixed label.
distractors: Rules still validate and enforce limits in ML systems; labels do not make them useless.
Plenty of labels makes classical ML viable; it does not force a deep model.
Needing no training data helps you start, but at volume a trained classifier is usually cheaper and easier to measure.

mcq.q: A keyword rule routes support emails to six teams, but paraphrased complaints such as “I was charged twice” keep landing in General. The team has 20,000 labelled emails. Which next step does the topic's example support?
options: Fine-tune a generative model to write replies instead of routing them
Add keyword rules until every paraphrase has a rule of its own
Prompt an LLM for a free-text team name and route on its exact words
Train a classifier on the labelled emails and compare it with the rule
mcq.why: Rules are brittle when wording changes. With 20,000 labels, classical ML (or a fine-tuned encoder for harder paraphrase) learns the variations cheaply, and the rule is the baseline to beat.
distractors: The problem is routing; writing replies does not put the email in the right team.
Paraphrases are open-ended; the rule set grows without end and stays brittle.
An LLM can route, but its label must be validated against the allowed teams, not used as free text.

interview.q: Explain the difference between AI, machine learning, deep learning and generative AI to a product manager.
covers: They are nested sets: each is one way of doing the outer one
Where the knowledge comes from: written rules, labelled examples with chosen features, learned features, a learned data distribution
Output type: a label or number versus open-ended content
One concrete example of the same task done each way
interview.followUp: Where does a hand-written fraud rule fit in that picture?

interview.q: What is the practical difference between classical machine learning and deep learning?
covers: Who designs the features: the engineer versus the network's layers
Data and compute needs
Typical fit: tabular data versus text, images and audio
Interpretability and cost trade-offs
interview.followUp: When would you still pick classical ML for a text task?

interview.q: Why is evaluating generative output harder than evaluating a classifier?
covers: Many valid answers instead of one correct label
Needs rubrics, checks, or human and model judges
Open-ended output can contain unsupported claims
So evaluation design starts before building (chapter 8)
interview.followUp: How would you evaluate an LLM that writes refund emails?

interview.q: A stakeholder wants “AI” to route support tickets. How would you choose between rules, a trained classifier and an LLM?
covers: Whether labelled data exists and how much
Volume and cost per ticket
Accuracy on rare but important categories
Starting with a baseline and measuring against it
Using an LLM to bootstrap labels when none exist
interview.followUp: What would make you switch from the LLM to a trained classifier later?

interview.q: Describe a system that combines several of these techniques. Which part fails most often, and how would you find out?
covers: Clear component boundaries
Per-component metrics and logs
Tracing a single bad output through each step
Attributing cost per component
interview.followUp: Several components share one request. How would you split its cost between them?

interview.q: {company}'s returns flow uses a rule, a risk model and an LLM-written reply. A shopper was wrongly refused a return. How would you find the cause?
covers: Check the eligibility rule and its inputs first
Check the risk score and the threshold used
Separate the decision from the wording of the LLM's message
Use per-component logs to reproduce the case
Add the case to a regression test
interview.followUp: Once you find the cause, how do you stop the same wrong refusal from coming back?

interview.q: Design a ticket-routing service that starts with an LLM and moves to a trained model as labels accumulate.
covers: LLM labels constrained to the allowed set, with validation
Logging predictions and human corrections as training labels
Training a classifier once enough labels exist, then comparing in shadow mode
Fallbacks and per-ticket cost tracking
Keeping the LLM for rare or ambiguous cases
interview.followUp: How many labels would you want before switching, and how would you decide?

interview.q: {company} must show an auditor why a card payment was declined and what the customer was told. What would you log, and for which component?
covers: The rule checks with their inputs and versions
The fraud score, model version and threshold
The LLM's prompt version, inputs and the message sent
Stable request IDs linking all three
Retention and access controls for the logs themselves
interview.followUp: A year later the auditor asks you to replay the decision. What must you have kept to do it?

mcq.q: What limitation of rule-based expert systems did statistical machine learning address?
options: Rules could only be written once enough labelled data had been collected
Rules needed constant network access to look up facts while running
Rules broke on cases they did not anticipate and became unmaintainable
Rules ran too slowly because they needed GPUs that did not yet exist
mcq.why: Expert systems worked in narrow domains but broke on anything unanticipated; learning weights from data made systems more robust to noise and variation.
distractors: Rules are written by people; labelled data is what statistical ML needs.
Expert systems ran locally on their own rule base; network access was not their limit.
Rules are cheap to run; GPUs mattered later, for training neural networks.

mcq.q: What was the main remaining limitation of statistical ML before deep learning?
options: Engineers still had to hand-design the features
It needed reinforcement learning to reach useful accuracy
It only worked on images, not on text or tabular data
It could not learn weights from data, only follow rules
mcq.why: Statistical models learned weights, but people still decided the features (for example “count of exclamation marks”). Deep networks learn features themselves.
distractors: Statistical ML used supervised methods such as naive Bayes and SVMs, not reinforcement learning.
Spam filters on text were a classic statistical ML success.
Learning weights from data is exactly what statistical ML introduced.

mcq.q: What changed in 2012 that made neural networks take off?
options: Transformers were published and replaced convolutional networks for images
Backpropagation was invented, so multi-layer networks could finally be trained
The first chat assistant was released and showed what neural networks could do
GPUs and large labelled datasets let deep networks win ImageNet by a wide margin
mcq.why: Backpropagation was popularised in 1986; the breakthrough came when GPUs and large datasets arrived, shown by AlexNet in 2012.
distractors: Transformers came in 2017, five years later.
Backpropagation was popularised in 1986; it was not the 2012 change.
Chat assistants came after instruction tuning, around 2022.

mcq.q: Why were RNNs and LSTMs slow to train on large datasets?
options: They cannot represent text, so it must first be converted to images
They have so many parameters that each step needs several GPUs
They attend from every token to every other token at each step
They process tokens strictly in order, which limits parallelism
mcq.why: Recurrent networks carry a hidden state from token to token, so steps cannot run in parallel across the sequence.
distractors: RNNs were built for sequences such as text; they read one token at a time.
Their limit was sequential computation, not parameter count.
That describes attention in a transformer, which is what made training parallel.

mcq.q: What did the 2017 transformer remove compared with earlier sequence models?
options: Recurrence: every token attends to every other token in parallel
The need for training data: it learns language from the architecture
Attention: it kept only the feed-forward layers and dropped attention
Learned parameters: its attention weights are fixed rules, not trained
mcq.why: “Attention Is All You Need” removed recurrence and kept attention, which suits GPUs and scales to huge datasets.
distractors: Transformers need very large datasets; the architecture alone knows nothing.
The paper is “Attention Is All You Need”: attention is the core, recurrence is what went.
All of a transformer's weights, including attention projections, are learned.

mcq.q: What defines a foundation model?
options: One large model pretrained on broad data, then adapted to many tasks
A rule-based system with thousands of rules written by domain experts
A model trained only on one company's data for that company's tasks
Any neural network with more than one layer, whatever its training data
mcq.why: Foundation models (BERT, GPT-2, GPT-3) are pretrained once on broad data and adapted to many tasks by prompting or fine-tuning.
distractors: That is an expert system, the first era.
Narrow, single-owner training is the opposite of broad pretraining.
Depth alone makes a deep network, not a foundation model; broad pretraining and reuse define it.

mcq.q: What made foundation models follow instructions well enough to become chat assistants?
options: Instruction tuning and RLHF
Training on fewer tokens
Adding hand-written rules for every question
Removing attention
mcq.why: Around 2022, instruction tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback turned pretrained models into assistants.
distractors: Instruction following came from extra tuning, not less pretraining.
Chat assistants are not built from per-question rules.
Attention remained central.

mcq.q: Which statement about agents is accurate?
options: An agent is an application architecture: a model in a control loop that calls tools
An agent proves the model reasons like a person, since it plans its own steps
An agent is a new kind of neural network layer that is trained to call tools
An agent replaces the language model with a planner written as fixed rules
mcq.why: An agent is a design pattern: the model chooses actions, observes results and decides next steps in a loop.
distractors: Planning steps in a loop is a design pattern; it says nothing about human-like reasoning.
Tool calls come from the application loop around the model, not from a new layer type.
The LLM is the decision-maker inside the loop; agents are built around it.

mcq.q: In the example sentence “The movie was not bad at all”, why might a bag-of-words classifier get the sentiment wrong?
options: It always predicts positive for short sentences with few words
“bad” carries a negative weight and word order is ignored
It cannot read English words that it did not see during training
It attends from “bad” to “not”, but the attention weight is too small
mcq.why: A bag-of-words model sums word weights without order, so “not … at all” does not flip “bad”.
distractors: Bag-of-words has no rule about sentence length; it sums word weights.
“not” and “bad” are common words; unseen words are not the problem here.
Bag-of-words has no attention; that is how a transformer handles this sentence.

mcq.q: A support team already has keyword rules, a trained classifier and a RAG answerer. A new agent workflow is proposed. What does the history of the field suggest?
options: The agent should replace the rules, classifier and RAG answerer at once
Retrieval is unnecessary once an agent can call tools and plan its steps
Rules became obsolete once trained classifiers could learn from data
Each stage fixes a specific failure; earlier stages often stay useful
mcq.why: Each era solved the previous one's main limitation without making it useless. Rules and classifiers are still cheaper and more exact for some jobs.
distractors: Replacing working parts adds risk without fixing a named failure.
Agents still need retrieval to get facts; tool calls often are retrieval.
Rules still do exact checks and permissions better than any model.

mcq.q: A claims team maintains 4,000 IF–THEN rules, and every new product line breaks several of them in ways nobody predicted. Which shift from the history of the field addresses this?
options: Running the same rules on GPUs, the change that made deep networks win in 2012
Adding attention so that each rule can look back at the rules before it
Learning weights from labelled claims instead of writing every rule by hand
Asking the rule writers to use a stricter format so rules cannot conflict
mcq.why: Expert systems broke on cases the rules did not anticipate, and thousands of rules became unmaintainable. Statistical ML replaced hand-written rules with weights learned from data.
distractors: GPUs speed up training neural networks; they do nothing for rules that miss new cases.
Attention is a mechanism inside neural networks, not a way to organise written rules.
A stricter format keeps rules tidy, but people still have to anticipate every case.

mcq.q: An LSTM sentiment model handles “not bad at all” but misses negations that sit hundreds of tokens before the verdict, and it takes days to train on the team's corpus. Which change addresses both problems?
options: A bag-of-words classifier, which ignores word order and trains much faster
A rule that flips the sentiment whenever “not” appears anywhere in a review
A deeper LSTM with more gates, so it carries its memory over longer spans
A transformer, where every token attends to every other token in parallel
mcq.why: LSTMs read tokens strictly in order, which is slow to train, and still forget over long distances. Attention turns a long-range link into a direct lookup, and transformers compute it for all tokens in parallel.
distractors: It trains fast but ignores order, so it loses the negation entirely.
Brittle: “not only great but…” would be flipped wrongly, as rule systems always were.
Still sequential, so still slow, and gates only reduce forgetting over long distances.

interview.q: Walk me through the main eras of AI and the limitation each one solved.
covers: Rules broke on the unanticipated
Statistical ML learned weights but needed hand-made features
Deep learning learned features, enabled by GPUs and data
Attention and transformers replaced sequential processing with parallel attention
Foundation models, instruction tuning, then agents
interview.followUp: What limitation did transformers bring that later work still has to deal with?

interview.q: Why did transformers replace RNNs for language?
covers: Parallel processing across the sequence suits GPUs
Direct attention between distant tokens instead of a chain of hidden states
Scales to very large datasets
RNNs forget over long distances and train slowly
interview.followUp: What did transformers give up compared with RNNs, for example on very long inputs?

interview.q: What is a foundation model and why did it change how teams build AI products?
covers: Pretrained once on broad data
Adapted to many tasks with prompts or fine-tuning
Teams start from a capable model instead of collecting task data first
Capabilities improved with scale
interview.followUp: When would you still train a task-specific model instead of adapting a foundation model?

interview.q: A colleague says agents are a new kind of neural network. How would you respond?
covers: An agent is a control loop around a model
Tools, observations and decisions are application code
Risks come from actions, not architecture
Limits, approvals and evaluation are still needed
interview.followUp: Which agent risks would you test before giving it write access to a system?

interview.q: Give an example where an older technique is still the right choice today, and explain why.
covers: A concrete task such as permissions, tabular fraud scoring or exact search
Cost, exactness, auditability or latency advantage
How you would show the newer approach is not better
When you would revisit the choice
interview.followUp: What evidence would make you switch to the newer approach?

interview.q: {company} moved from a search form to an agent that books trips. What new risks did that introduce, and how would you control them?
covers: Partial bookings and the need for undo (sagas)
Duplicate actions on retries
Spending money without approval
Limits on steps and cost
Evaluating whole workflows, not single answers
interview.followUp: The flight is booked but the hotel step fails. Walk me through the recovery.

interview.q: Your team wants to replace a working keyword-plus-classifier support router with an LLM agent. How would you decide?
covers: Measure the current system's accuracy, cost and failure cases first
Define what the agent must do better
Run it in shadow on real traffic
Compare cost per correct routing
Keep the old system as a fallback
interview.followUp: What result would make you stop the migration?

interview.q: How would you explain to leadership why “just use the newest model” is not an architecture?
covers: Each component has a job: rules, retrieval, models, tools
New models change capabilities, not requirements
Evaluation decides, not novelty
Cost, latency and risk constraints still apply
interview.followUp: Leadership asks you to pick a model anyway. How do you decide?

mcq.q: What is a hallucination?
options: Fluent, confident output that is false
Any output that the user dislikes or rejects
A slow response that times out before finishing
A refusal to answer a question it could answer
mcq.why: When the model lacks a fact, a plausible-sounding fabrication is still the likely continuation.
distractors: A correct answer can be disliked; hallucination is about falseness.
Latency is a serving problem, not a hallucination.
Over-refusal is a separate failure; a hallucination is a confident false answer.

mcq.q: Why does a model not know about your product release last week?
options: It only reads English, and the release notes are translated
It deletes memories older than its context window allows
Release notes are too long to fit into its parameters
Its weights reflect data up to a training cutoff
mcq.why: Knowledge in the weights is frozen at the cutoff, and your internal documents were never in training at all unless supplied in context.
distractors: Language is not the issue; the release happened after the training data was collected.
Weights are not deleted over time; they are frozen at training.
Parameters are not a store that documents are put into; new facts reach the model through the context.

mcq.q: An assistant invents a configuration flag that does not exist. Which mitigation does the topic recommend?
options: Raise the temperature so the model samples other flag names and picks the best
Ask the model to double-check its own answer before replying, in the same prompt
Retrieve the real docs, require a quote from them, and add the case to the eval set
Switch to a model with more parameters, which has seen more configuration files
mcq.why: Supply the facts, constrain the answer to cite them, and keep the case as a regression test.
distractors: More sampling produces more plausible-looking fabrications, not the real flag.
The model has no new information to check against; it will often confirm the same invented flag.
Your gateway's docs were not in its training data; size does not supply missing facts.

mcq.q: Why is “I'm certain” from a model not a usable control signal?
options: It only appears in English, so it cannot be used for answers in other languages
Models are never certain, so the phrase is filtered out before the reply is sent
It is always false: a model says it only when it has no supporting evidence
Tone does not track correctness until confidence is measured against labelled cases
mcq.why: Even token probabilities are only loosely related to factual accuracy after instruction tuning; measure calibration before relying on any confidence.
distractors: The issue is not language; tone carries no information about correctness in any language.
Nothing filters the phrase; models say it freely, which is why it must not be trusted.
It is not reliably false either; it simply carries no information until measured.

mcq.q: Which of these are practical limitations described in the topic? Choose all that apply.
options: Inability to translate
Non-determinism
Arithmetic and exact counting errors
Sensitivity to prompt wording
mcq.why: Counting errors (tokens are not characters), wording sensitivity and non-determinism are listed. Translation is listed as a strength.
distractors: Translation is one of LLMs' strengths.

mcq.q: A model screens job applications. Which limitation becomes a legal and ethical problem?
options: Bias learned from skewed training data
Long context windows that include whole CVs
Slow decoding when many applications arrive
A large vocabulary that splits rare names
mcq.why: Associations learned from the world's skews can treat groups differently, which matters in hiring, lending and moderation.
distractors: Context length is a cost and capacity concern, not a fairness problem.
Throughput is an operations problem with no legal dimension.
Vocabulary size affects token counts, not fair treatment of candidates.

mcq.q: Which limitation does retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mainly address?
options: Poor tokenisation of non-English text in your documents
Bias learned from skewed data in the model's weights
Non-determinism, so the same question gets one answer
Missing or outdated knowledge of your own documents
mcq.why: RAG puts current, private facts into the context. It does not change the weights, so bias and randomness need other controls.
distractors: Tokenisation is fixed by the model; retrieval does not change it.
Retrieval supplies facts; it does not change biases in the weights.
Retrieval does not make sampling deterministic.

mcq.q: An answer comes with a citation. What must you still check?
options: That the citation is formatted in the style the team agreed on
That the cited passage is long enough to be a reliable source
Nothing more, because a citation proves the claim is supported
That the cited passage actually supports the specific claim
mcq.why: Models can attach real sources to unsupported claims, so grade support claim by claim.
distractors: A well-formatted citation can still point to a passage that says something else.
Length says nothing about whether the passage supports this claim.
Models can attach real citations to unsupported claims.

mcq.q: Why do models often miscount the letters in a word?
options: They see tokens, not individual characters
Letters are removed from words during training
They cannot count at all, even small numbers
Counting needs a GPU that inference does not use
mcq.why: A word may be one or a few tokens, so the characters inside are not directly visible.
distractors: Training keeps the text; it is split into tokens, which hide individual letters.
They count small sets of tokens reasonably; the problem is that letters are inside tokens.
Inference runs on the same hardware; the limit is how the text is represented.

mcq.q: Which test case best catches stale-knowledge failures in a policy assistant?
options: A question about a policy that was revised last week
The same question asked twice in a row, to compare
A question about the most frequently asked policy
A greeting followed by a request for the policy list
mcq.why: A recently revised policy shows whether the system answers from the current version or from older knowledge.
distractors: Repeating a question tests consistency, not whether knowledge is current.
Common, stable policies are the least likely to expose stale knowledge.
A greeting tests conversation handling, not stale facts.

interview.q: What are the main limitations of LLMs, and where does each come from?
covers: Hallucination from predicting likely text
Stale knowledge from a training cutoff
Bias from skewed training data
Unreliable confidence
Counting errors, wording sensitivity, injection
interview.followUp: Which of these can you fix in your application, and which only by changing the model?

interview.q: What is the difference between a hallucination and outdated knowledge?
covers: Hallucination: plausible fabrication when a fact is missing
Outdated: a fact that was true at the cutoff but has changed
Both are fixed by supplying current facts
Tests need different cases for each
interview.followUp: Write one test case for each, for a policy assistant.

interview.q: Why should you not trust a model's stated confidence?
covers: Tone does not track correctness
Token probabilities are loosely related to accuracy after tuning
Confidence must be calibrated on labelled cases
Use measured signals instead
interview.followUp: What does a reliability diagram show that a single accuracy number does not?

interview.q: How would you design an evaluation set to catch hallucinations in a policy assistant?
covers: A policy that does not exist
A recently revised policy
Questions needing two documents
Questions in other languages
Grade support per claim, not fluency
interview.followUp: How big does the set need to be before you trust a difference between two prompts?

interview.q: The assistant cites a real source, but the claim is wrong. How does that happen, and how do you catch it?
covers: Citations can be attached without support
Retrieval returned a related but wrong passage
Check claim-level support automatically and by sampling
Track the rate over time
interview.followUp: How would you measure claim-level support without reviewing every answer by hand?

interview.q: {company} must give the same answer to a customer in English, Hindi and Tamil. How would you test and monitor that?
covers: Parallel test cases in each language
Compare extracted facts (amounts, deadlines), not wording
Per-language failure rates
Monitor the production language mix and quality by language
interview.followUp: Tamil answers fail twice as often as English ones. Where do you look first?

interview.q: Design guardrails for an LLM that answers questions about fees, limits and refunds.
covers: Retrieve only the current policy version
Require citations and verify numbers against the source
Refuse or escalate when no source is found
Human review for high-risk cases
Log and evaluate continuously
interview.followUp: Where would you put a human in the loop, and how would you size that queue?

interview.q: How would you decide whether a model's confidence can be used to route answers to human review?
covers: Build a labelled set of correct and incorrect answers
Plot a reliability diagram
Pick a threshold from review capacity and risk
Re-check calibration after model or prompt changes
interview.followUp: After a model upgrade, how would you notice that calibration has drifted?
